rawScriptText:
Your Liver Is Under Attack
Every Night You Eat Late.
Primary: Oxford University — Cell Metabolism, Mar 2026  |  Supporting: UCSD — Sleep, Mar 2026  |  Depth layer: Kumar et al. — Indian Journal of Sleep Medicine, 2026  |  Format: Short-form vertical, 55 seconds

Studies powering this script
Primary anchor
Fatty liver as a diurnal, circadian-driven disease
Oxford University · Cell Metabolism · Mar 2026
Supporting layer
Time-restricted eating reduces fasting blood glucose
UCSD · Sleep · Mar 2026
Depth layer
Sleep medication independently linked to elevated blood glucose
Kumar et al. · Indian Journal of Sleep Medicine · 2026
Production brief
Hook mechanic
Fear reframe — timing not food
Tone
Composed, clinical, credible
Duration
55 seconds
Key stat
9-hour eating window
Silent risk
Sleep meds raise glucose
CTA style
Comment trigger ("LIVER")

Scene-by-scene breakdown
0:00 – 0:07
Scene 1 — Cold open / hook
Hook
Visual direction
Creator visible in near-darkness — only refrigerator light or a single lamp. Clock or phone shows 11 PM. No food props needed; the setting does the work. Hold the frame for a beat before speaking. No music intro — silence first.
Voiceover
"Fatty liver disease is not just about what you eat. A study out of Oxford, published in March 2026, found it is primarily about when your liver processes fat — and the most dangerous window is while you sleep."
On-screen overlay
Not what you eat.
When you eat.
Oxford · Mar 2026


0:07 – 0:18
Scene 2 — The science (circadian mechanism)
Science
Visual direction
Talking head under cool-toned blue light — reinforces the nighttime frame. Optional: a clean animated graphic of a clock overlaid on a liver silhouette showing fat accumulation peaking at night. Keep any graphic minimal and text-light.
Voiceover
"Here is the mechanism. Your liver's fat production is circadian — it naturally ramps up at night, while insulin sensitivity drops. Eating in that window overloads a system that was designed to be in recovery mode, not processing mode."
On-screen overlay
Liver fat peaks at night
Insulin sensitivity — lowest
Circadian mismatch


0:18 – 0:30
Scene 3 — The silent risk (sleep medication)
Reveal
Visual direction
B-roll: a pill bottle on a bedside table — understated, not dramatic. Cut to a glucose monitor reading. Creator back to camera, serious but not alarmist. This scene should feel like a doctor speaking frankly, not a scare tactic.
Voiceover
"And a 2026 study in the Indian Journal of Sleep Medicine added something most people have never heard: in otherwise healthy adults, regular use of sleep medication was independently linked to elevated blood glucose — even with no diagnosis of diabetes. The pill helping you sleep may be quietly disrupting your metabolic health."
On-screen overlay
Sleep meds

↑ blood glucose (p < 0.001)
No diabetes required
Narrative pivot. Scenes 1–3 build the problem: late eating disrupts liver function, and sleep medication may further compromise glucose control. Scene 4 delivers the solution — time-restricted eating — so the video ends on agency, not anxiety. The emotional arc is: curiosity → quiet alarm → clarity → control.

0:30 – 0:44
Scene 4 — The intervention (TRE + walking)
Solution
Visual direction
Creator holds a simple hand-drawn or printed timeline: 9 AM to 6 PM highlighted, rest blacked out. Then cut to B-roll of a kitchen light switching off, a pantry door closing. Quick, clean. No dramatic effects needed.
Voiceover
"The intervention that directly counters this is a 9-hour eating window. A concurrent 2026 study in the Sleep journal showed that time-restricted eating in this format meaningfully reduced fasting blood sugar. Finish eating by 6 PM. Your liver gets the overnight recovery window it was designed for."
On-screen overlay
Eat: 9 AM → 6 PM
9-hour window
Fasting glucose — down


0:44 – 0:50
Scene 5 — Closing frame / series link
Bridge
Visual direction
Back to talking head, warm lighting now — a deliberate shift from the opening darkness. Signals resolution. Posture open, not leaning in. One breath before speaking.
Voiceover
"This is part of a pattern — the same pattern we covered with postprandial walking and sleep extension. Timing and movement are the two levers that metabolic science keeps returning to in 2026."
On-screen overlay
Timing + Movement
The 2026 metabolic formula


0:50 – 0:55
Scene 6 — CTA
Call to action
Visual direction
Stay on talking head. No pointing at the screen. Drop the energy one notch — this should feel like the end of a conversation, not a commercial break. Let the comment trigger feel organic.
Voiceover
"Comment 'LIVER' below and I will send you a full breakdown of all three studies. Three papers. One framework. Exactly what the research says to do."
On-screen overlay
Comment: LIVER
3 studies · 1 framework
Credibility note for the creator. Study 3 (Kumar et al.) is a cross-sectional study — it shows association, not causation. The voiceover reflects this accurately ("linked to," not "causes"). Do not upgrade the language in post-production. For a creator of this profile, precision in scientific framing is a long-term brand asset. The finding is genuinely significant (p < 0.001) and newsworthy on its own — it does not need overstatement.

Director notes
Lighting
The opening dark-room shot is the visual identity of this script. Refrigerator light, a desk lamp, or practical side-lighting only. This is not an aesthetic choice — it physically anchors the viewer to the "nighttime = danger" thesis before a word is spoken. The warm-light close is equally deliberate: it signals safety and resolution.
Structure
Three studies, one argument. Oxford defines the problem (circadian fat accumulation). Kumar et al. adds the sleeping pill finding as an unexpected second risk. UCSD provides the solution. This is the same architecture as Script 2: the viewer receives one complete insight, not three separate ideas in a trench coat.
Pacing
Scenes 1 and 2 are slower — the science is dense and the atmosphere is doing work. Scene 3 (sleep meds) should land quietly, not dramatically. A pause before "even with no diagnosis of diabetes" is more effective than emphasis. Scene 4 picks up pace. Scenes 5 and 6 decelerate to close.
Series link
Scene 5 references Scripts 1 and 2 explicitly — postprandial walking and sleep extension. If the creator has published those videos already, this line earns the callbacks and rewards returning viewers. If not, cut "the same pattern we covered" and replace with "a pattern that 2026 metabolic science keeps confirming."
Caption copy
Cite all three studies: (1) Oxford — Cell Metabolism, Mar 2026, circadian fatty liver. (2) UCSD — Sleep, Mar 2026, 9-hour TRE and fasting glucose. (3) Kumar P. et al. — Indian Journal of Sleep Medicine, 2026, Vol. 21(1) — sleep medication and blood glucose. IJSM link: ijsm.in. Note study 3 is cross-sectional (association, not causation). Include the p < 0.001 statistic — it signals rigor to informed readers.
Comment DM
The "Comment LIVER" CTA implies a DM response. Prepare a short breakdown message in advance: one sentence per study, one unified takeaway, all three links. Respond within the first 2 hours for algorithmic benefit and to reinforce the creator's reputation for follow-through.

#FattyLiver
#CircadianRhythm
#TimeRestrictedEating
#IntermittentFasting
#MetabolicHealth
#OxfordResearch
#SleepMedication
#BloodSugarControl
#LiverHealth
#HealthScience2026

Suggested caption hook (first line)
"Oxford researchers just confirmed that fatty liver is a circadian disease — and your evening habits are the trigger. Here is what three 2026 studies say to do instead."
Series placement note. This is the natural third chapter of a metabolic health arc: Script 1 established postprandial walking, Script 2 debunked sleep extension alone, Script 3 completes the framework with circadian eating and the sleep medication risk. Together they form a cohesive playlist with a single unified prescription — move after meals, eat in a window, protect sleep quality without pharmacological dependency.

rawScriptText:
The 30-Day Protocol That
Science Actually Proved Works.

Primary: Marjot et al. — Cell Metabolism, March 3, 2026 (Oxford & Melbourne)  |  Activation: Zaghzi & Derbal — Academic Journal of Social and Human Studies, Jan 2026  |  Format: Short-form vertical, 45 seconds

Studies powering this script
Mechanistic anchor
MASLD is a diurnal disease driven by nighttime insulin resistance & reduced insulin availability
Marjot et al. · Oxford & Melbourne · Cell Metabolism · Mar 3, 2026
Clinical proof
Walking + sugar-free 16/8 IF produces measurable glucose & BMI reductions in 30 days
Zaghzi & Derbal · Academic Journal of Social & Human Studies · Jan 2026
The two-step protocol
Step 1
Postprandial walking
10 minutes immediately after each meal. Muscles absorb blood glucose before insulin has to work. Clinically validated in 30-day case study.
Step 2
Sugar-free 16/8 fasting
Eat within an 8-hour window. No added sugar. Cuts nighttime liver fat accumulation at its circadian peak. Resets insulin sensitivity.

Production brief
Hook mechanic
Protocol reveal — immediate utility
Tone
Energetic but grounded
Duration
45 seconds
Key result
Glucose + BMI down in 30 days
Oxford layer
Explains the mechanism why
CTA goal
Save + return in 30 days

Scene-by-scene breakdown
0:00 – 0:06
Scene 1 — Cold open / protocol hook
Hook
Visual direction
Creator holds a simple 30-day calendar — no red marker theatrics, just a clean visual prop. Confident, still. Speak before moving the prop, not while holding it up. The stillness signals authority. Natural daylight only.
Voiceover
"A 2026 clinical study gave a Type 2 diabetic patient two instructions. Thirty days later, her blood sugar had dropped significantly, her BMI fell, and her physical capacity improved. Here is exactly what she did — and why Oxford University's latest research explains why it works."
On-screen overlay
2 instructions.
30 days.
Measurable results.

0:06 – 0:18
Scene 2 — Step 1: postprandial walking
Protocol
Visual direction
B-roll: creator walking at a purposeful pace — outdoors, pavement, natural environment. Not a gym, not a treadmill. The visual must feel accessible. POV shot of feet moving works well here. Keep cuts fast — 2 to 3 seconds each.
Voiceover
"Step one: walk immediately after every meal. Not an hour later. Immediately. When you walk postprandially, your muscles pull glucose directly from your bloodstream — before your pancreas has to respond. It is one of the most efficient metabolic interventions in the current literature."
On-screen overlay
Step 1: Walk after meals
Muscles absorb glucose
No gym required


0:18 – 0:30
Scene 3 — Step 2: sugar-free 16/8 fasting
Protocol
Visual direction
Pantry or kitchen door closing — clean, deliberate, not dramatic. Then cut to a simple graphic: a timeline bar with an 8-hour eating window highlighted in green. Keep the graphic minimal — white background, one colour. No animation needed.
Voiceover
"Step two: compress your eating into an 8-hour window and remove all added sugar. Oxford University published research in March 2026 showing that liver fat accumulation and insulin resistance peak at night — meaning every calorie eaten late compounds the problem. Closing the window early gives your liver its recovery period."
On-screen overlay
Step 2: 16/8 fasting
Zero added sugar
Oxford · Cell Metabolism 2026

Why the Oxford study belongs in this script. Marjot et al. (Cell Metabolism, 2026) provides the mechanistic explanation for why Step 2 works — nighttime insulin resistance and hepatic lipogenesis are circadian-driven and persist even after weight loss. This is not filler; it upgrades the protocol from "a case study found this" to "a landmark Oxford paper explains the biology behind why this works." For a large creator, this distinction is the difference between a trending video and a credibility-building video.

0:30 – 0:40
Scene 4 — The clinical proof
Evidence
Visual direction
Talking head — creator holds phone showing a clean line graph of glucose declining over 30 days. Do not show a real patient's data; create a simple illustrative graphic. The prop grounds the abstract result in something visual and concrete.
Voiceover
"In the clinical case study, a Type 2 diabetic woman followed both steps for one month. Fasting blood glucose fell significantly. BMI dropped. Functional physical capacity improved. The researchers concluded this is a viable non-pharmacological first-line intervention — their words, not mine."
On-screen overlay
Fasting glucose — down
BMI — down
"Non-pharmacological" — the study


0:40 – 0:45
Scene 5 — CTA close
Call to action
Visual direction
Talking head, same framing as Scene 4. No dramatic energy shift — keep it grounded. The CTA should feel like a natural close, not a gear change into presenter mode. One beat of silence before the last line lands harder.
Voiceover
"Save this. Start tomorrow. And come back in 30 days — because the study says 30 days is enough to see something real."
On-screen overlay
Save this video
Start tomorrow
30 days → report back
Credibility note — single-subject study. The Zaghzi & Derbal case study has an n of 1, which is clinically interesting but not a large-scale trial. The voiceover handles this correctly by describing it as a "case study" and using "significantly" only where the data supports it. Do not upgrade language in post to "proven" or "clinical trial" — those terms imply a scale this study did not reach. The Oxford paper (Marjot et al.) is the rigorous anchor; the case study is the human story. Both are needed. Neither should be overstated.

Director notes
Energy
This is the most action-oriented script in the series — but "energetic" for a high-profile creator means confident and purposeful, not high-tempo or breathless. The pacing is brisk but the delivery is grounded. Think informed expert, not hype reel. The protocol's simplicity is the excitement; the creator's job is to convey how simple it actually is.
Oxford use
The Oxford study (Marjot et al.) is not a separate topic — it is the reason why Step 2 works. It should be woven into Scene 3 as explanation, not flagged as a second study. Viewers should leave thinking they learned one integrated protocol, not two separate pieces of research.
30-day CTA
The "come back in 30 days" close is the strongest long-term engagement mechanic in this series. It creates a commitment loop — the viewer saves the video, attempts the protocol, and has a reason to return. Consider pinning a follow-up reminder post at day 15. If the creator collects audience responses at day 30, that material becomes the next video.
No pills line
The original brief included "no expensive pills required" — this has been removed from the VO. For a credible large-scale creator, that framing reads as anti-medicine positioning, which risks alienating viewers managing T2D with medication. The study itself uses the phrase "non-pharmacological first-line or complementary therapy" — use that instead. It is clinically accurate and does not imply that medication is bad.
Cite method
Caption should cite both studies in full. For Marjot et al.: PubMed PMID 41529695, Cell Metabolism, March 3, 2026. For Zaghzi & Derbal: Academic Journal of Social and Human Studies, January 2026, ASJP link. Note the case study is n=1. Transparency on study scale builds long-term trust with a sophisticated audience.
Series arc
This script functions as the actionable payoff of the four-video series. Scripts 1–3 built the science. Script 4 says: here is exactly what to do with it. If the creator is posting these as a series, Script 4 should reference the earlier videos in the caption, not in the video itself — the VO should stand alone for new viewers arriving cold.
#Type2Diabetes
#PostprandialWalking
#IntermittentFasting
#GlucoseControl
#MetabolicHealth
#OxfordResearch
#30DayChallenge
#WeightLossProtocol
#DiabetesManagement
#HealthScience2026

Suggested caption hook (first line)
"Two steps. Thirty days. A 2026 clinical study showed measurable drops in blood sugar and BMI — and Oxford's latest research explains exactly why the biology works."
Four-video series — complete arc
Script 1
Walking after meals lowers blood sugar — the 30-day case study
Script 2
Sleeping more won't fix insulin resistance without movement
Script 3
Your liver is under attack every night you eat late
Script 4
The complete 30-day protocol — what to do and why it works

Walk after meals.

Education

Talking-head close up. Creator gestures deliberately — pointer finger, counting motions. Optional: animated graphic of blood glucose curve flattening after a post-meal walk. Clean, readable text on screen.

Scene 3 — The protocol revealed
Proof
Visual direction
B-roll: a clock graphic showing 16/8 intermittent fasting window, then a calendar marked with a simple 30-day streak. Keep visuals clean and black-and-white with one accent color — reinforce simplicity.
Voiceover
"The researchers combined postprandial walking with a 16-eight intermittent fasting window — and they cut out all added sugar. Thirty days. Significant results. BMI down. Fasting glucose down. Physical fitness up."
16 / 8 fasting window
30 days → results

0:30 – 0:42
Scene 4 — Practical takeaway
Action
Visual direction
Creator walking casually outdoors — after breakfast, after lunch. POV shot of feet on pavement. Timer graphic: "10 min." Keep it relatable and achievable — no gym, no gear.
Voiceover
"You do not need a gym. You do not need expensive supplements. A ten-minute walk after your next meal is a clinical-grade metabolic intervention. Start tonight."
10 min walk = clinical impact
No gym needed

Call to action

Voiceover
"The full study is in the caption. And if someone you know is managing their blood sugar — send this to them right now. It could genuinely change something."
Full study — in caption
Share with someone who needs this

Director notes:

For the creator:

Tone
You are the trusted friend who happens to know science. No hype, no alarm — just grounded authority. Speak slightly slower than your natural pace on the clinical terms. Let the facts do the emotional work.
Wardrobe
Neutral, elevated basics — no logos. The credibility is in your delivery, not your branding.
Prop idea
Open with a glucose meter or a post-meal walk in frame. Immediate visual signal that this is real, not abstract.
Caption copy
Credit the study fully: "Study: Zaghzi & Derbal (2026). The Effect of Walking and Sugar-free Intermittent Fasting on a Woman with Type 2 Diabetes. Academic Journal of Social and Human Studies." Include the ASJP link.
SFX / Music
Low ambient instrumental — no drops, no dramatic stings. The content is already compelling. Let silence do work in the hook's first two seconds.

rawScriptText:
Sleeping More Won't Save You.
Here Is What Will.
Primary study: Washington University — Diabetes Care, May 2026  |  Supporting study: Hallajzadeh et al. — Sleep and Breathing, February 2026  |  Format: Short-form vertical, 45 seconds

Studies used in this script
Primary anchor
Sleep extension & insulin sensitivity in overweight short-sleepers
Washington University · Diabetes Care · May 2026
Supporting layer
Ultra-processed foods, sleep latency & daytime dysfunction in older adults
Hallajzadeh et al. · Sleep and Breathing · Feb 2026

Production brief
Hook mechanic
Myth bust — belief reversal
Tone
Calm authority, zero alarm
Duration
45 seconds
Key stat
+1.1 hrs/night, 6 weeks
Twist
Sleep improved. Insulin didn't.
CTA goal
Follow for daily science

Scene-by-scene breakdown

0:00 – 0:06
Scene 1 — Cold open / hook
Hook
Visual direction
Creator sits upright in bed — no alarm energy, no comedy. Smartwatch visible on wrist showing a solid sleep score or 9 hrs. Look directly into camera. Deadpan. No smile yet.
Voiceover
"Nine hours of sleep. Every night. And your insulin resistance is exactly the same. A study published in May 2026 just explained why — and the answer is not what most people expect."
On-screen overlay
9 hrs sleep
Still insulin resistant?

0:06 – 0:16
Scene 2 — The study setup
Data
Visual direction
B-roll: glucose monitor reading, coffee being poured in the morning. Then cut to a clean animated graphic — a sleep bar growing by 1.1 hours. Simple, readable. No clutter.
Voiceover
"Researchers took overweight adults who were chronically sleep-deprived and had them sleep an extra 1.1 hours every night for six full weeks. Their sleep scores improved meaningfully. Their bodies felt better."
On-screen overlay
+1.1 hrs/night
6-week trial
Overweight adults

0:16 – 0:27
Scene 3 — The result (the reveal)
Reveal
Visual direction
Talking head. Creator holds one deliberate finger up — not theatrical, just grounded. Optional: a split graphic showing sleep score improving on one side, insulin marker flat-lining on the other.
Voiceover
"But their muscle insulin resistance — unchanged. Their liver insulin resistance — unchanged. Sleep extension alone did not move the metabolic needle. Not even slightly."
On-screen overlay
Sleep score — improved
Insulin resistance — unchanged

Narrative pivot point — where Study 2 enters. At this moment the creator layers in the UPF finding: ultra-processed food disrupts sleep architecture even when sleep duration increases — meaning bad food choices can silently undercut whatever sleep gains the viewer thinks they are making. This adds depth without derailing the primary study's conclusion.

0:27 – 0:38
Scene 4 — The real fix (action layer)
Action
Visual direction
Fast cuts: walking shoes on pavement, a clean meal without packaged food, someone stepping outside after dinner. No gym. No effort-signalling. Keep it effortlessly achievable.
Voiceover
"A separate 2026 study found that ultra-processed foods — even when sleep duration is fine — are independently wrecking your sleep quality and your daytime function. So the full picture is this: sleep more, move after meals, and cut the processed food. Not one. All three."
On-screen overlay
Sleep more
Walk after meals
Cut ultra-processed food

0:38 – 0:45
Scene 5 — CTA close
Call to action
Visual direction
Talking head. Lean slightly forward — close, direct, no performative energy. No pointing at the follow button like a TV presenter. Say it like a smart friend would say it.
Voiceover
"Both studies are in the caption. Follow if you want the science without the noise — one study, one takeaway, every day."
On-screen overlay
Studies — in caption
Follow for daily science

Director notes
Narrative
This script runs two studies as one coherent argument — not two separate topics. Study 1 (Washington) delivers the myth bust. Study 2 (Hallajzadeh) deepens it. The viewer should feel like they received one insight with two layers of proof, not two different videos stitched together.
Pacing
Scenes 1–3 are slower and deliberate — let the surprising result land. Scenes 4–5 pick up pace. The edit rhythm should mirror the emotional arc: curiosity → confusion → clarity → resolution.
Hook note
Do not open with energy or a question. Open with a statement that assumes the viewer already holds the wrong belief. "Nine hours of sleep. Still insulin resistant." That assumption is the scroll-stopper — it makes anyone who has tried to fix their health through sleep feel called out instantly.
Gender note
Study 2 found gender-specific differences: UPF intake linked more to daytime dysfunction in women, sleep latency in men. This is worth a brief line in the caption for audience depth, but do not include it in the video — it fragments the message at 45 seconds. Save it for a follow-up.
Caption copy
Credit both studies: (1) Washington University, Diabetes Care, May 2026 — sleep extension and insulin sensitivity. (2) Hallajzadeh et al., Sleep and Breathing, Feb 2026 — ultra-processed foods and sleep quality. Springer link: link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11325-026-03688-x. Note that both studies are peer-reviewed. Include the gender-specific UPF finding as a bonus detail for engaged readers.
